title: Lyman and the umbrella; his habit of calling keys
summary: Lyman's fear of umbrellas and brooms, and how Williams followed his raised hand through key changes using about 300 songs.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: You were talking about the rainy night there and you came in with umbrellas and all that, raincoats there, with Tommy Lyman. Go ahead. I got it. Well, in the morning it was time to go home,

when he see an umbrella, he jumped from here to that next room. He says, you bore the hell out of me. He says, my brothers went out, what do you call them? High-heft boots. High-button shoes. High-button shoes. And we were waking up at the piping rock, the porter comes along in the morning, sweeping along in the bar, see. He said, you let me get a drink then. You want a drink of this? Yeah, so. I drink beer. So I get a beer. And along comes the porter sweeping the floor with all the small brooms. And he sees that broom, he misjumped me across the street. That's how superstitious he was. Now listen, he wasn't too hard for me to play for. He liked me because I knew maybe 300 songs. And he did too, see. And Reese Haber-Herschel at the Brill Bill and that was Jack Tempsey's restaurant. And that's a building full of records, where they make records and stuff. And I had some fellas come in and listen to Tommy and I. So I wouldn't do that. I said, what do you mean? Tommy and I would start out, I was born in Virginia, but they'd go about 10 bars. And he raises his hand up, and I go from F to F sharp. And he says, in D wrote, uh, uh, there's a girl in the heart in Maryland. And that's in B flat, up his hand and puts me in five sharp. And he goes into Indy Road, Georgia, in my southern home, one of those things. And before I get through him playing five flats, the half a tone of key above C is five flats. And they go, and nothing could be fine in Sweetie Carolina in the morning. That's the kind of guy, no matter how I continue. We have a rehearsal, maybe twice a month, and he'd have three songs. You can't take no music on the job. Now that's, you got to have it there to learn all the numbers. See? Yeah. Oh, it was wonderful.
